title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Primary cutaneous lymphomas are a heterogeneous group of T- and B-cell neoplastic entities impacting millions of individuals worldwide annually. In 2018, the World Health Organization updated the diagnostic criteria for the various subtypes of this group of tumors to assist dermatologists and pathologists in classifying them. Cutaneous B-cell lymphomas (CBCLs) are often distinguished clinically by their indolent behavior. Prominent dermal B cell infiltrates are often present, which is remarkable because B cell collections are not typically found in normal skin and are rarely observed in reactive conditions or other types of CL. The following activity outlines the evaluation of these tumors and highlights many pathologic underpinnings when managing patients with primary cutaneous lymphomas.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify all subtypes of cutaneous T- and B-cell lymphomas according to updated World Health Organization guidelines. Summarize general histopathologic features of cutaneous T- and B-cell lymphomas. Outline immunophenotypic and molecular findings of cutaneous lymphomas. Review pertinent clinicopathologic findings associated with different cutaneous T- and B-cell lymphomas. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Introduction
content: Primary cutaneous lymphomas are a heterogeneous group of skin-based non-Hodgkin lymphomas that lack extracutaneous manifestations at diagnosis and are the second most common type of extranodal lymphoma. [1]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Introduction
content: In 2018, the World Health Organization–European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (WHO-EORTC) published an updated classification of cutaneous lymphomas in the 4th edition of the WHO Classification of Skin Tumors Blue Book, which serves as the gold standard in the diagnosis. [2] Primary cutaneous lymphomas more frequently originate from a T-cell than a B-cell lineage. [3] In the Western world, cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) make up approximately 75% of all cutaneous lymphomas, with the majority classified as Mycosis fungoides. [4] Around 6.4 per million persons worldwide are affected by CTCL, and the likelihood of the disease increases significantly with age. [5] The median age at diagnosis is approximately 54 years, although it may rarely occur in children and adolescents. [6] [7]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Introduction
content: Patients with CTCL have increased risks of secondary cancers such as other non-Hodgkin lymphomas, melanoma, lung cancer, and bladder cancer. [8] When neoplastic Mycosis fungoides cells are found in the blood, the condition is known as Sézary syndrome. [9] Primary cutaneous lymphomas are often complex and require clinical evaluation, light microscopy, immunohistochemistry, and molecular analysis of skin biopsies. [10]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Issues of Concern
content: According to the Prospective Cutaneous Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (PROCLIPI) study published in 2020, patient characteristics associated with a significant decrease in quality of life (QoL) in Mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome include being newly diagnosed and having alopecia and confluent erythema. [12]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Issues of Concern
content: In 2021, a published study of 1-on-1 patient interviews suggests that those with CTCL, such as Mycosis fungoides, often report sleep interference, lack of understanding of their disease, feelings of uncertainty, depression, hopelessness, treatment/tumor burden, and sometimes suicidal thoughts. [13] Overall, diminished health-related QoL is observed in both patients with CTCL and CBCL, particularly those with advanced-stage disease, and this is well documented in the current literature. [14]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Causes
content: UV radiation is a risk factor for CTCL, as supported by multiple studies and genetic evidence. [15] [16] [17] Except for adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), an aggressive peripheral T-cell lymphoma caused by the human T-lymphotropic virus type-1 (HTLV-1) and presenting with skin findings in approximately half of cases, epidemiologic studies have failed to identify or associate environmental or viral causes with most CTCL subtypes. [18] [19] However, certain medications, such as hydrochlorothiazide, may induce significant antigen-driven CTCL after chronic exposure (ie, greater than 1 year). [20] [21]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Causes
content: As with most cases of CL/CTCL, the cause of CBCL remains incompletely understood. However, chronic antigenic stimulation is a potential etiology, perhaps due to specific infectious agents such as Borrelia burgdorferi, Helicobacter pylori, and Epstein-Barr virus. [22] [23] [24] [25] [26]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology
content: Histology is vital to the diagnostic evaluation and workup of cutaneous lymphoma, and growth patterns differ between CTCL and CBCL. The former often demonstrates atypical T-cell lymphocyte infiltration of the epidermis (epidermotropism). In contrast, the latter typically presents with dense dermal B-cell lymphocyte infiltrates (as described above) without significant epidermal involvement. [11] [27] See Images. Epidermotropism (CTLC), Dense B-Cell Dermal Infiltrate (CBCL).

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology
content: Six major anatomic/histologic patterns occur in CL: epidermotropic, nodular, diffuse, subcutaneous, angiocentric/angioinvasive, and intravascular. Epidermotropic infiltrates are commonly observed in the early stages of most CTCLs (eg, Mycosis fungoides, patch, and plaque stages). In contrast, nodular and diffuse infiltrates are more common in later stages of CTCL (eg, Mycosis fungoides, tumor stage) and in CBCL. Subcutaneous growth suggests subdermal cutaneous lymphomas (eg, SPTCL). Angiocentric/angioinvasive infiltrates are seen primarily in primary cutaneous gamma/delta and aggressive NK-cell/T-cell cutaneous lymphomas, but may also be present in less-aggressive CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (eg, LyP, Type E). Intravascular growth, finally, can be seen in intravascular anaplastic large cell, large B-cell, NK-cell, or pseudolymphomas. [27]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Mycosis fungoides/SS: Band-like papillary dermal infiltrate with epidermotropism (patch stage) and formation of Pautrier's microabscesses (collection of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis), atypical lymphocytes with 'cerebriform' nuclei in the upper dermis and epidermis (plaque stage), or diffuse dermal lymphocyte infiltrate (tumor stage). See Image. Pautrier Microabscesses. Lymphocytes may tag along the dermo-epidermal junction. Reactive, inflammatory skin changes (eg, spongiosis) are typically absent. [28] The papillary dermis exhibits wiry collagen. IHC: CD3+, CD4+, CD5+/-, CD7-, CD25+/-, CD30+/-, CD56-, CCR4+. [29] Mycosis fungoides variants

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: FMF: Atypical lymphocyte infiltrate surrounding hair follicles (folliculotropism) with follicular mucinosis. Hair follicles may be intact, destroyed, or have cysts with or without basaloid folliculolymphoid hyperplasia. It may be accompanied by eosinophils, granulomatous dermatitis, or perieccrine infiltrates (syringotropism). [30] [31] IHC: CD3+, CD4+, CD8-, with an elevated CD4:CD8 ratio (6-10:1); CD30 may be positive in large cell transformation. [31] [32]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Pagetoid reticulosis: Epidermal atypical mononuclear (pagetoid) cell hyperplasia with eosinophilic cytoplasm. A dermal mixed inflammatory infiltrate with or without CD8+ epidermotropism may also be present. IHC: variable CD4, CD8, and CD30 expression; Ki-67/MIB1 may show active proliferation, but is not specific. [33] [34] [35]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: GSS: Diffuse loss of elastic fibers, non-caseating granulomatous T-cell infiltrates in the upper dermis, and multinucleated giant cells may all be present. [36] [37] IHC: CD4+/45RO+/30+; multinucleated giant cells, often CD68+, and may have surrounding CD1a+ cells. [38] [39] [40]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: ATL: Dermal tumor cell lymphocyte infiltrate with occasional epidermotropism. Patterns may vary from resembling Mycosis fungoides to C-ALCL, or peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS. [29] [41] IHC: CD3+, CD5+, CD45RO+, CD8+/-, CD25+/-, CD30+/-, CD7-, CD20-, CD79a-; elevated Ki-67 may be present in more aggressive forms of ATL. [42] Primary cutaneous CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorders

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: C-ALCL: Large, irregular polygonal lymphocytes in sheets throughout the dermis. Epidermotropism with or without subcutaneous or adnexal involvement may be present. Cutaneous lymphatic infiltration may be present. The "hallmark" feature of eosinophilic cells with horseshoe nuclei is not always present. IHC: CD30+ membranous and Golgi pattern expression in over 75% of tumor cells. Cytotoxic phenotype (ie, CD8, TIA-1, granzyme, perforin) positivity may occur in angioinvasive cases. [2] [43] [44]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: LyP: (Type A) Wedge-shaped CD30+ tumor cells in scattered or clustered patterns with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. (Type B) Epidermotropic CD30+/- tumor cells with cerebriform nuclei (resembling Mycosis fungoides). (Type C) Sheets of large CD30+ atypical lymphoid cells with minimal reactive inflammatory cells. (Type D) Epidermotropic small- to medium-sized CD8+ and CD30+ tumor cells (resembling CD8+ AECTCL). (Type E) Large necrotic "eschar"-like lesions with angioinvasion secondary to CD8+ and CD30+ co-expressed atypical lymphocytes. IHC: CD3+, CD4+, CD25+, CD30+, CD45RO+, CD56+/-, CD2-, CD3-, CD5-, CD7-. CD8 positivity, as opposed to CD4 positivity, is more frequently observed in Types D and E. [2] [45]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Extranodal NK-cell/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type: Pleomorphic atypical lymphoid cells primarily limited to subcutis with angioinvasion and extensive connective tissue/blood vessel necrosis. IHC: CD3+, cytotoxic granules+, CD56+, CD43+/-, CD45RO+/-, CD4-, CD8-, CD16-, CD57-. [46]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: CAEBV infection: Cutaneous and subcutaneous adipocyte necrosis with septal atypical lymphocyte infiltrate; Reed Sternberg-like cells may be present in an NK-cell variant. [47] IHC: EBV+ lymphocytes with EBER positive signaling (>100/HPF); atypical T-cells may express CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, TIA-1, or GRB (negative for CD2, CD56); Ki-67 positivity may show active proliferation. title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: CD4+ SMT-LPD (provisional): Nodular to diffuse atypical dermal lymphocytes without epidermotropism and surrounded by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. IHC: CD3+, CD4+, PD-1+, BCL6+, CXCL3+, CD8-, cytotoxic granules-. [29] [49]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Primary cutaneous acral CD8+ T-cell lymphoma (provisional): Diffuse dermal atypical lymphocyte infiltrate without epidermotropism. IHC: CD3+, CD8+, CD4-, CD30-, CD56-, TIA-1+, EBER-ISH-. [29] [49]
contents: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma. Primary cutaneous acral CD8+ T-cell lymphoma (provisional): Diffuse dermal atypical lymphocyte infiltrate without epidermotropism. IHC: CD3+, CD8+, CD4-, CD30-, CD56-, TIA-1+, EBER-ISH-. [29] [49]

content: Primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS: Remaining aggressive T-cell lymphoproliferative histologic entities which do not fit other established CTCL categories (namely CD4+ SMT-LPD, CD8+ AECTCL, and PCGDTL). [49] [50]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
content: PCMZL: Nodular or diffuse dermal lymphoplasmacytoid or monocytoid marginal zone B-cells with or without T-cells. Lymphoid follicles may be present. IHC: CD20+, CD79a+, BCL2+, BCL6-, CD5-, CD10-, CD16-. [29] [49] See Image. Dermal Plasma Cells.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
content: PCFCL: Dense proliferation of neoplastic follicular central B-cells ("centrocytes") separated from the epidermis by a Grenz zone and exhibiting a background dendritic meshwork. The Ki-67 proliferation index is low. It may have surrounding reactive T-cells. IHC: CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD79a+, PAX5+, BCL6+, CD10+/-, BCL2-. [51]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
content: PCDLBLC, LT: Diffuse dermal sheets of monomorphic large B-cells with open chromatin and prominent nucleoli. The proliferation lacks background dendritic meshwork and shows a high proliferation index. IHC: CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD79a+, PAX-5+, BCL2+, IRF4/MUM-1+, FOXP1+. [52]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Anatomical Pathology -- Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
content: EBVMCU (provisional): EBV+ atypical large B cells resemble the morphology of DLBCL and classic Hodgkin lymphoma. A mixed inflammatory infiltrate may be present. Reactive T-cells may surround B-cell clusters. IHC: CD15+, CD30+, CD19+, CD22+, CD79a+, PAX-5+, EBV+, IRF4/MUM-1+, CD20+/-, CD10-, BCL6-. [2] IVBCL: Large atypical B-cells with large nuclei and varying nucleoli demonstrating intravascular proliferation/destruction. IHC: CD79a+, CD20+, IRF4/MUM-1+, CD5+/-, CD10+/- , CD29-, CD54-. [53]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Pathology
content: T- and B-cell clonality studies are necessary ancillary tests to support the diagnosis of CTCL and CBCL, respectively, especially when distinguishing hyperplasia from monoclonality. The use of primers targeting genes such as IGH , IGK , IGL , TRG , and TRB is up to 90% sensitive for detecting most types of CL. However, these tests must be used in conjunction with clinical, histologic, morphologic, and immunophenotypic data.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Pathology
content: Clinical follow-up may be indicated in certain patients whose clinical and anatomic pathologic findings do not correlate initially with cutaneous lymphoma. Dermatopathologists may request additional samples from skin biopsies of different lesion sites when uncertain. Linking results from gene rearrangements in skin biopsies with those from peripheral blood samples may also increase the reliability of these tests. [54]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Pathology
content: Although circulating atypical Sézary cells may be present in cases of Mycosis fungoides, peripheral blood smear evaluation is necessary for patients with suspected Sézary syndrome (eg, older age, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, generalized pruritus). [55] Furthermore, positivity for PD-1 (CD279) and KIRDL2 (CD158k) biomarkers can provide additional data to help differentiate Sézary syndrome from other erythrodermic inflammatory dermatoses in the skin and peripheral blood. [2] [56] [57]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Pathology
content: Alongside establishing definitive atypical, neoplastic T-cell monoclonal populations in the skin and blood, an absolute Sézary cell count of >1000/microliter in the peripheral blood with expanded CD4+ T cell population resulting in a CD4/CD8 ratio ≥ 10, CD4+/CD7- cells ≥ 30%, or CD4+/CD26− cells ≥ 40% is necessary to establish a diagnosis of Sézary syndrome, according to the 2018 WHO-EORTC. [2]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Pathology
content: In patients with suspected ATL, a peripheral blood smear showing “flower” or “cloverleaf” cells (polylobated T-cells with condensed chromatin) is pathognomonic. HTLV-1 infection should be confirmed by ELISA (highest sensitivity), Western blot, or PCR. Recommended cytologic panel evaluation includes CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD25, and CD30. [58] [59] Patients with EBV-associated cutaneous lymphomas (eg, CAEBV infection, EBVMCU, extranodal NK-cell/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type) require confirmation of viral infection for definitive diagnosis. [60]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Pathology
content: In patients with CBCL and lymphocytosis, peripheral blood flow cytometry is recommended, and bone marrow biopsy is indicated for those with disseminated skin disease or lymphadenopathy. In any patient with PCDLBCL-LT, both peripheral blood flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy are recommended, given this condition’s poor prognosis compared to other CBCL subtypes (5-year survival of about 50%). [49]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Biochemical and Genetic Pathology
content: Although monoclonality detected by molecular analysis may help diagnose cutaneous lymphoma, its presence does not necessarily indicate malignancy, nor does its absence rule it out. [27] Analysis of antigen receptor genes (ARGs) via rearrangement studies, such as IGH, is a functional assay that helps determine and distinguish cutaneous lymphomas from other lymphoproliferative entities. [61]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Biochemical and Genetic Pathology
content: Targeting mutations in genes involved in the MYC, BCL6, NF-κB, and JAK-STAT signaling pathways, among others, may assist and serve as critical ancillary tests when working up CTCL and CBCL. [2] [62] Several notable markers are discussed in the "Clinical Pathology" section of this topic. This aspect of cutaneous lymphoma evaluation is continually evolving as research elucidates the underlying etiologies.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations
content: Clinicopathological correlation is essential when establishing a diagnosis of cutaneous lymphoma subtype, as most cutaneous lymphomas exhibit similar histology and immunophenotypes. [27]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Mycosis fungoides: Presents as erythematous patches, plaques, tumors, or erythrodermic “stages,” most frequently involving non-sun-exposed “bathing suit” areas in older individuals. Lesions may accompany epidermal atrophy, scaling, or pruritus. Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches/plaques may be present, particularly in patients with skin of color. It rarely presents in children or adolescents (Mycosis fungoides variants are more common in this population). [63] [64] Mycosis fungoides Variants

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: FMF: Presents as grouped erythematous patches, plaques, and tumors accentuated around follicles on the neck and face (especially eyebrows). Patients often have alopecia (up to 81%), comedones, or rosacea-like skin changes. Although the mean age of onset ranges from 46 to 59 years (higher in men than in women), FMF is a common variant of juvenile Mycosis fungoides. [65]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Pagetoid reticulosis: Localized Pagetoid reticulosis, also known as Woringer-Klopp disease (WKD), presents as solitary, hyperkeratotic, verrucous, or psoriasiform plaques on the extremities of patients between their third and 6th decades of life. As with FMF, Pagetoid reticulosis may present in pediatric patients. [34] [66] Widespread Pagetoid reticulosis, also known as Ketron-Goodman disease, is more aggressive. Ketron-Goodman disease and metastatic Pagetoid reticulosis are more challenging to treat and have higher mortality rates. [67] [68]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: GSS: Presents as erythematous, pruritic lax skin and wrinkles, mainly in flexure/axillary regions in men during their third to 4th decades of life. Plaques may be violaceous with atrophy and have mild desquamation. [36] [37]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Sézary syndrome: Presents more frequently in older persons as generalized erythroderma (ie, greater than 80% body surface area) with exfoliation, edema, pruritus, or lichenification. Lymphadenopathy is common. [9] Skin classification, stage of disease, elevated LDH, advanced age, comorbidities, race, male sex, peripheral eosinophilia, and large cell transformation are all associated with a worse prognosis. [69]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: ATL: Presents as large, rapidly growing cutaneous papules, nodules, or tumors. [70] ATL is caused by HTLV-1, which affects around 10 million people worldwide annually. It is endemic in Japan, the Caribbean, Africa, the Middle East, South America, and Central America. Rapidly progressive disease is associated with chemotherapeutic resistance, immunosuppression, and an overall poor prognosis. [71] [72] [73] Primary cutaneous CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorders

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: C-ALCL: Presents as solitary, grouped, or multifocal (approximately 20% of the time) nodules or tumors that often persist for at least 3 to 4 weeks. Superficial ulceration may be present and frequently involves the extremities and face (less commonly the trunk). Cutaneous relapse may occur, and partial or complete regression happens in about 25% of patients. Most commonly, C-ALCL arises in patients aged 50-70 years, but it may also occur in pediatric populations. [43] [74] Extensive involvement of the leg, skin, muscle, and deep fascia is associated with a poorer prognosis. [75] [76] [77] LyP: Presents as a benign, chronic, and often relapsing papulonodular eruption over the face, trunk, or limbs. Post-inflammatory hypopigmented macules and atrophic scars may occur at sites of spontaneous resolution. [45] Older age and T-cell monoclonality are significant risk factors for secondary cutaneous lymphoid malignancies (eg, Mycosis fungoides, C-ALCL, and Hodgkin lymphoma). [78] [79]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: SPTCL: Often presents as multiple, relapsing, self-healing subcutaneous nodules on the trunk or extremities. Nodules are painless and may occur in the same or different locations on the skin. About 75% of patients have multifocal skin involvement. Associations of SPTCL include serosal effusions, hemophagocytosis, and pancytopenia. [80]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Extranodal NK-cell/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type: Often presents as ulcerating, necrotizing, or destructive lesions on the midface, nose, or upper airways. Surrounding edema and erythema may frequently occur. It is most common in Asia and Latin America, and among similar heritage groups. Positive EBV detection via in situ hybridization (ISH) is necessary to confirm the diagnosis. [46]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: CAEBV infection: According to the 2018 WHO-EORTC classification, this diagnosis includes EBV+ lymphoproliferative disorders (LPD) in childhood, which are classified into 2 subtypes: hydroa vacciniform-like LPD (HV-like LPD) and severe mosquito bite allergy (sMBA). [81] [82] HV-like LPD: Presents as a papulovesicular eruption on sun-exposed skin areas (eg, face, ear lobes, back of hands) with or without systemic symptoms (eg, fever, lymphadenopathy). Extensive non-sun-exposed skin involvement, facial swelling, and extensive ulcers may indicate disease severity. sMBA: Presents as ulceronecrotic lesions at the site of mosquito bites with similar systemic symptoms as seen in patients with HV-like LPD. This condition is most common in children and young adults, and patients of Asian or Hispanic descent. Primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma, rare subtypes

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: PCGDTL (provisional): May present as diffuse superficial patches and plaques on the extremities with or without facial tumor ulceration. Lesions may appear similar to Pyoderma gangrenosum on the legs, deep nodules on the trunk, or in conjunction with Mycosis fungoides-like plaques on non-sun-exposed skin areas. It is more likely to present in adults aged 40 to 70 and has a poor prognosis. [83]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: CD8+ AECTCL (provisional): May present as Pyoderma gangrenosum-like lesions or PR-like patches and plaques with hyperkeratosis. Lesions may appear as annular or erythematous widespread papules, plaques, and ulcerated tumors without precursor lesions. They tend to appear suddenly and rapidly within weeks to months and may be locally aggressive. They occur most commonly on acral skin surfaces; oral involvement indicates a poor prognosis. The age of presentation is broad, from young adults to the elderly. [84]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: CD4+SMT-LPD (provisional): Commonly presents as asymptomatic, solitary, slow-growing violaceous or erythematous papules, plaques, nodules, or tumors. Most cases involve the head and neck, followed by the trunk and upper extremities. Pain or pruritus may occur, but ulceration is rare. Although these occur predominantly in elderly persons in the 6th and 7th decades of life, pediatric patients may also be affected. [85]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Primary cutaneous acral CD8+ T-cell lymphoma (provisional): Presents most commonly in adult males older than 50 as solitary, slow-growing nodules on the ear, although they may occur on the nose, hands, and feet. Symmetrical skin involvement is common, and the disease typically has an indolent course. [86]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma
content: Primary cutaneous peripheral T-cell lymphoma, NOS: May present as solitary erythematous to violaceous tumors or nodules throughout the body. Ulceration and subsequent infection may occur, and rapid dissemination with systemic symptoms is not uncommon. The prognosis is abysmal, with a 5-year disease survival rate of less than 20%, and is more likely to appear in older adults/elderly persons. [50]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
content: PCMZL: Typically presents as pink, red, or violaceous papules, plaques, or nodules. They commonly occur on the arms or trunk rather than on the head and neck, and predominantly affect adult males aged 50 to 60. However, they are rare cases of cutaneous lymphoma among children and adolescents. [87] PCFCL: Presents as 1 or more localized, erythematous papules, plaques, or tumors on the scalp, forehead, or trunk of adult males 50 to 60 years old. [51]

content: PCDLBLC, LT: Often presents as rapidly developing red to plum nodules or tumors on 1 or both legs of older women (median age of diagnosis is 70 years old). This condition frequently metastasizes to extracutaneous sites, including lymph nodes and bone marrow, and warrants further hematopathologic evaluation given its poor prognosis. [52]

content: EBVMCU (provisional): Appears as shallow, well-circumscribed mucosal or cutaneous ulcers with indolent disease progression. Most patients experience spontaneous regression. The median patient age at presentation is approximately 66 years, with a slight female predominance. [88]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinicopathologic Correlations -- Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma
content: IVBCL: A rare subtype of DLBCL with intravascular involvement leading to blood vessel destruction and necrosis. Lesions may occur anywhere in the body, but skin involvement is more common in individuals from Western populations. Constitutional B symptoms may also occur. Disseminated disease most commonly affects elderly persons around 70 years old without gender predilection. [53]

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Significance
content: In light of discussions from the 2021 Clinical Advisory Committee (CAC) and recognition of updated WHO guidelines, the 2022 International Consensus Classification (ICC) of lymphomas continues to acknowledge the frequent evolution of cutaneous lymphoma subtype classification.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Significance
content: Clinically, accurate diagnosis of the specific cutaneous lymphoma subtype is essential, as different entities exhibit distinct clinical behaviors and prognostic implications. Practitioners should recognize that many cutaneous lymphoma subtypes share overlapping histopathologic features, which is significant because dermatopathologists rely heavily on the presentation and features of clinical lesions (ie, clinicopathologic correlation) to determine the most accurate cutaneous lymphoma subtype diagnosis for each patient.

title: Dermatopathology, Cutaneous Lymphomas -- Clinical Significance
content: Although a complete understanding of cutaneous lymphomas remains incomplete, continued collaborative large-scale cohort studies and advances in biomolecular detection technologies (eg, genetic and epigenetic) may help dermatopathologists, dermatologists, and other practitioners in characterizing and further subclassifying these entities to provide high-quality patient care. [89]
